source.title: Margin-Based Generalization for Quantum Machine Learning with Classical Data Encoding
source.authors: Junghee Ryu; Tak Hur; Daniel K. Park

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether margin and parameter-based measures track generalization gaps in quantum neural networks trained on classical image data, extending generalization-measure evaluations to a new model family.
record.gate_note: The paper reports aggregate comparisons of complexity measures against generalization gaps over 19,440 QNN training runs. These findings concern margin-based prediction of gaps, not the specific classical-network claims in V1–V8.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates margin and parameter-count predictors of generalization gaps in simulated QNNs. None of V1–V8 is tested: in particular, V7 names magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness in convolutional networks, which this study never measures. Random-label fitting is cited from other studies; varying batch size does not supply a fixed-epoch batch-size comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's empirical paraphrase is substantially accurate: inverse median margin is strongest among the principal baseline and bound-derived measures, while empirical margin loss performs better still. The globally tuned composite's tiny sign-error advantage is within uncertainty. Architecture-specific weights retain a small held-out advantage on five axes, so parameter terms should not be described as universally useless. The authors also derive generalization bounds for fixed and trainable classical-data encodings.
record.recipe_differences: Quantum neural network simulations on binary classical image tasks; evaluates margin and parameter-based predictors of generalization gaps rather than the listed classical-network interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Predictor rankings vary by measure and criterion; parameter-count measures are constant on embedding, batch-size, learning-rate, and dataset changes. The composite measure's sign-error result depends on in-sample tuning; its small global-weight advantage is within bootstrap uncertainty. Empirical margin loss results vary by margin level.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 19,440 simulated QNN runs, inverse median margin scores better than the baseline parameter-count measures. Its K is 0.004565 versus 0.0001932 for parameter count; corresponding 90th-percentile sign-errors are 0.7124 and 0.7724. Every baseline nevertheless has environments with sign-error 1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-margin measures predict QNN generalization-gap orderings better than the tested parameter-count measures in these binary image tasks, with substantial failures in some environments.

fits_no_version.finding: The global composite's in-sample sign-error advantage is only 0.0007, with a paired interval including zero; both bound-derived measures have lower K than inverse median margin.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding bound-derived parameter-count terms supplies little robust predictive improvement over inverse median margin in this QNN grid.

fits_no_version.finding: Empirical margin loss outperforms inverse median margin at all three tested margin levels. At γ=0.1, the paired sign-error difference is −0.0069 with 95% interval [−0.0111,−0.0034].
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Lower-tail training-margin information predicts QNN generalization gaps better than inverse median training margin in these experiments.

record.problems: The study uses simulated QNNs and three binary image tasks with images reduced to two PCA features. Several training and test gaps are small and can be comparable to finite-test-set fluctuations. The 12 architecture-specific composite weights are tuned in-sample for the reported 0.6988 result; authors note that this may be optimistic. Conditional-independence confidence intervals use only five random seeds and are described as coarse.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported result was omitted from the extracted aggregate metric comparisons. Figure 3's per-hyperparameter 90th-percentile sign-errors are presented as figure values without a complete numeric table and were not extracted as rows; Table 1 and the text report the aggregate comparisons and describe the parameter measures' limitations by hyperparameter.

untested.parts: No own comparison of fixed random-label fitting, natural-label generalization, and random-label held-out chance performance.
No test-error trajectory beyond the width needed for interpolation in one-hidden-layer ReLU networks.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison or local-connectivity intervention.
Adam is used throughout; no optimizer comparison or tuning-budget comparison.
Batch sizes vary, but training stops by convergence rather than a fixed epoch budget; no directional held-out batch-size penalty or recovery result is reported.
No magnitude-aware weight perturbations, sharpness measurement, convolutional-network comparison, or sharpness ranking against norm and margin measures.
No memorization-based example identification, removal, or retraining comparison.

record.verdict_notes: All rows remain linked to none; their states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8, not judgments that the reported predictor comparisons are unreadable. These comparisons can be retained under fits_no_version. No missing result bearing on a listed version was identified in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare fitting fixed random labels with generalization on natural labels.
Does not test width beyond the interpolation threshold in one-hidden-layer ReLU networks.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected classical networks.
Uses Adam but does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD for generalization.
Varies batch size but does not report a small-versus-large batch generalization comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
Evaluates margins and parameter-based measures, not magnitude-aware sharpness or weight perturbations.
Does not identify or remove memorized training examples.
